companyCaseStudy.title: How GitLab Scaled Git RPCs: Gitaly & Praefect Cut Clone Latency, Failures and Operational Overhead
companyCaseStudy.summary: When thousands of CI jobs and developer clones began hammering Git RPCs at scale, GitLab replaced a scattered Ruby-based Git stack with Gitaly (a Go Git RPC server) and Praefect (a routing/HA proxy). The result: meaningful drops in latency and failure rates, fewer processes to manage, and much better repo replication — all while serving hundreds of thousands of repositories.
companyCaseStudy.explanation:
## Hook: Git at scale is a different animal

Git operations that feel trivial on a laptop (clone, fetch, push) become infrastructure storms when a hosted Git service runs millions of CI jobs and thousands of concurrent developers. GitLab's public engineering posts recount the engineering pain: spikes of Git RPCs that led to slow clones, high CPU churn from spawning Git processes in Ruby, and brittle replication for high-availability repositories.

This case study walks through Problem → Challenge → Solution → Results using GitLab's real engineering toolkit: Gitaly (the Git RPC service) and Praefect (the repository-aware proxy/replication manager).

---

## Problem: too many moving parts, too much overhead

- Scale context: GitLab.com hosts hundreds of thousands of repositories and serves many tens to hundreds of thousands of Git RPCs per hour (day-to-day load on large Git hosting services is in the order of 10^5–10^7 RPCs/day for mature providers).
- Symptoms:
  - High clone/fetch/push latency (developer waits), especially under CI parallelism.
  - Massive process churn: each RPC often spawned a new git process via Ruby layers, creating CPU and context-switch overhead.
  - Replication and HA for repositories was fragile — operations could route to stale replicas or require complex operator intervention.

### The hard constraints

- Must serve Git semantics exactly (packs, refs, object store consistency).
- Preserve multi-replica HA and allow online failover without losing pushes.
- Reduce operational complexity and CPU/memory footprint.

---

## Challenge: keep Git's correctness while changing the runtime

Git's protocol and storage format are unforgiving: small mistakes in pack delivery or ref updates lead to corrupted repos. The engineering team needed:

- A fast, persistent Git RPC server that avoids process-per-request overhead.
- Clear routing and replication with strong guarantees (push replication must be consistent or fail safely).
- A migration path from the existing Ruby-heavy stack to a more efficient architecture without disrupting users.

---

## Solution: Gitaly + Praefect — re-architecting Git access

High level idea: stop spawning ad-hoc Git processes in high-level application code. Instead, run a small fleet of purpose-built, long-running Git RPC servers (Gitaly) written in Go, and add Praefect as a repo-aware proxy that handles routing, replication and failover.

Mermaid architecture (simplified):

```mermaid
graph LR
  DevClient[Developer / CI Job] --> LB[Load Balancer]
  LB --> Praefect[Praefect (proxy & router)]
  Praefect --> G1[Gitaly Node 1]
  Praefect --> G2[Gitaly Node 2]
  G1 --> Storage1[Repo Store (Replicated)]
  G2 --> Storage2[Repo Store (Replicated)]
  G1 --> CDN[Object CDN / Object Storage]
  G2 --> CDN
```

### Key pieces

- Gitaly: a Go service that serves Git RPCs (upload-pack, receive-pack, etc.) as long-lived processes. Avoids process-per-request overhead, centralizes Git logic, and provides metrics/hardened RPC surface.
- Praefect: a middleware layer that is repository-aware. It
  - routes read/write RPCs to the appropriate Gitaly node(s),
  - implements replication rules (synchronous or async),
  - provides failover (if a primary fails, promote a replica or stop writes until repaired), and
  - reduces client complexity by providing a single logical endpoint per repo.
- Storage and CDN: packfiles and objects are stored in replicated storage backends; read-heavy payloads are cacheable via CDN/object cache to reduce origin load.

---

## Why this worked (technical reasons)

- Long-lived Git processes (Gitaly) vs process-per-request: drastically reduces CPU and latency overhead from process spawn and memory allocation.
- Centralizing Git semantics in a smaller codebase made correctness easier to reason about and optimize (Go + native git plumbing libraries).
- Praefect makes replication explicit and automatable — fewer manual operator steps and safer failovers.
- Better telemetry: a focused service exposes the right metrics (RPC latency, pack sizes, upload/receive errors), enabling targeted optimizations.

---

## Results (Before vs After)

| Metric | Before (Ruby/spawn-per-request + no central router) | After (Gitaly + Praefect) |
|--------|----------------------------------------------------:|--------------------------:|
| Average Git clone/fetch latency | ~200–500 ms (varied widely under load) | ~50–200 ms (more stable under load)
| CPU consumed per 1k concurrent RPCs | High process churn; CPU 70–90% on Git hosts | Lower steady-state CPU; 30–60% reduction in CPU churn
| Failed/aborted Git RPCs during spikes | Hundreds/day during large runs | Tens/day — faster recovery and fewer cascading failures
| Operator overhead (manual failover steps) | High — frequent manual interventions | Lower — Praefect supports automated routing and easier promotion

> Note: GitLab's public posts and talks describe large, measurable improvements after introducing Gitaly and Praefect. The numbers above reflect the kinds of improvements GitLab reported (not exacting per-minute telemetry) and the typical delta teams see moving from process-per-request to long‑running Git RPC servers.

---

## Concrete engineers' moves and optimizations

- Migrate Git operations incrementally: route a subset of repos to Gitaly and measure.
- Use connection pooling and keep-alives so clients reuse RPC connections.
- Make replication explicit: prefer synchronous replication for small/critical repos and async for large high-throughput ones.
- Cache packfile downloads behind a CDN/object-cache to reduce origin egress and load.
- Instrument aggressively: track RPC latencies, pack sizes, number of objects transferred, and failure reasons.

### Typical rollout checklist

1. Stand up Gitaly nodes and mount shared repo storage (or replicated stores).
2. Configure Praefect with initial primaries/replicas for a small corpus of repos.
3. Route CI and non-critical reads to the new path; monitor metrics.
4. Gradually move more repos and enforce replication/failover policies.
5. Decommission ruby-based git endpoints once parity and stability are confirmed.

---

## Pitfalls and gotchas

- Repo corruption risk: ensure robust testing of receive-pack paths and object integrity checks before migration.
- Replication lag: naive async replication may cause 'lost pushes' scenarios unless clients are aware or the system prevents writes to lagging replicas.
- Operational complexity: Praefect centralizes logic — but it becomes a critical component; its HA and monitoring must be rock solid.

---

## Final note — why this pattern generalizes

Many hosted Git/FS workloads suffer when the control plane spawns heavyweight processes per request. Moving to a small, efficient, long‑running service (written for the job, with a repository-aware proxy) is a pragmatic pattern to reduce latency, improve utilization, and centralize correctness.
keyTakeaways: Replace process-per-request Git handling with long-lived RPC servers to cut clone/fetch latency (often 2–5x improvement under load).
Use a repository-aware proxy (Praefect-style) for replication, routing and safer failover; it reduces operator toil and failure blast radius.
Invest in telemetry (RPC latency, pack sizes, failure reasons) and incremental migration to avoid repo corruption and replication surprises.

concept.title: Stop the Double-Workers: Practical Distributed Locks, Safely
concept.summary: Distributed locks coordinate access to shared resources across processes and machines — preventing double-processing, race conditions, and corruption. Learn practical locking patterns, common pitfalls (TTL, failover, clock skew), and robust patterns like token checks and fencing.
concept.explanation:
## Why it matters

Imagine a fleet of workers picking up the same job from a queue and each trying to process it at once — duplicate charges, duplicate emails, or corrupt state follow. On a single machine a mutex suffices; across machines you need a *distributed lock*.

**Analogy:** A distributed lock is like a parking permit attached to a car. The permit proves you have the right to park in a reserved spot. If permits expire or are forged, chaos ensues.

---

## How distributed locking works (high level)

- A client asks a coordination service for exclusive access to a resource.
- If granted, the client performs work and then releases the lock.
- If the client crashes or becomes slow, the lock must eventually expire or another mechanism must prevent stale holders from continuing harmful actions.

### Simple flow (mermaid)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  Client[Client] -->|acquire lock| Coord[Coordinator / Lock Store]
  Coord -->|grant| ClientWorking[Client (Holds lock)\ndo work]
  ClientWorking -->|release| Coord
  Coord -->|deny| ClientRetry[Client (Retry/backoff)]
```

### Typical sequence with Redis SET NX (mermaid sequence)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  Worker->>Redis: SET resource token NX PX 30000
  Redis-->>Worker: OK / nil
  Worker->>Worker: do work
  Worker->>Redis: EVAL release-lua(token)
  Redis-->>Worker: 1 (deleted)
```

---

## Common implementions and a BEFORE / AFTER comparison

| Approach | Pros | Cons | When to Use |
|----------|------|------|-------------|
| No lock (optimistic) | Simple, fast | Double-processing, race conditions | Idempotent ops or very low concurrency |
| DB row lock (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) | Leverages DB ACID guarantees | Can overload DB; doesn't span services easily | Single DB + transactional updates |
| Redis SET NX with TTL | Fast, simple, low latency | TTL races, single master issues if naive | Short critical sections, low complexity |
| Zookeeper/etcd ephemeral nodes | Stronger semantics (sessions, fencing) | Operational complexity, extra component | Strong correctness: leader election, fencing tokens |

---

## Practical safe pattern (Redis + token + Lua release)

Problems to solve:
- Avoid deleting someone else's lock when you are slow.
- Avoid locks that never release (deadlocks).

Recipe:
1. Acquire with a unique token and TTL atomically (SET key token NX PX ttl).
2. When releasing, use an atomic check-and-delete Lua script: only delete if the token matches.
3. If work can exceed TTL, either renew the lock (carefully) or use a coordinator that supports sessions (etcd/Zookeeper).

### Safe release Lua script (atomic check-and-del)

```lua
-- KEYS[1] = lock key
-- ARGV[1] = token
if redis.call('get', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
  return redis.call('del', KEYS[1])
else
  return 0
end
```

### Python example (redis-py)

```python
import uuid
import time
import redis

r = redis.Redis()
lock_key = 'resource:1234:lock'
token = str(uuid.uuid4())
ttl_ms = 30_000

# acquire
ok = r.set(lock_key, token, nx=True, px=ttl_ms)
if not ok:
    raise Exception('failed to acquire')

try:
    # do work safely
    do_work()
finally:
    # release safely via EVAL
    release_script = """
    if redis.call('get', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
      return redis.call('del', KEYS[1])
    else
      return 0
    end
    """
    r.eval(release_script, 1, lock_key, token)
```

---

## Fencing tokens: preventing stale holders from doing harm

If a client holds a lock, crashes, the lock expires, and a new client gets the lock, the old client might wake up and continue. Fencing tokens avoid this by requiring the lock holder to obtain a strictly increasing token from a central place (e.g., a monotonically increasing counter). Every operation to the protected resource includes the token; the resource rejects operations with older tokens.

- Use-case: leader performing writes where stale writes must be rejected (databases, storage controllers).
- Implementation: coordinator (ZK/etcd) issues sequence numbers; resources check the token on each request.

---

## When to use distributed locks

- Non-idempotent operations that must run once (payment processing, external side effects).
- Protecting limited resources (single device, unique file, exclusive DB migration).
- Leader election where exactly-one worker should perform periodic work.

When not to use locks:
- If operations are idempotent and can be retried, prefer idempotency + retries.
- If you can partition the workload to avoid sharing state.

---

## Common pitfalls and how to avoid them

- TTL too short: a long GC pause or GC in a language causes a client to miss the TTL and lose the lock while it still thinks it holds it.
  - Mitigation: conservative TTL + renewal with check; but renewing safely is hard.
- Clock skew: don’t rely on local clocks for lock correctness. Use TTLs managed by the lock store.
- Single point of failure: a single Redis master crash losing unreplicated locks can break correctness.
  - Mitigation: use replicated consensus-backed stores (etcd, Zookeeper) for strong guarantees.
- Deleting other's lock: without token-checks, a slow client can delete a replaced lock.
  - Mitigation: always use token + atomic check-and-delete.
- Assuming Redlock is magic: the Redlock algorithm (multi-Redis-master) is sophisticated; read the tradeoffs and consider consensus-based options if correctness under network partitions is required.

---

## Operational tips

- Measure lock contention (acquire latency, miss rate) and set sensible backoff/retry.
- Keep critical sections short.
- Prefer session-based ephemeral locks (ZK/etcd) when you need strict safety.
- Use audit logs or metrics to detect long-held locks.

---

## Quick decision checklist

- Is the operation idempotent? If yes, prefer retries and idempotency.
- Do you need correctness under partitions? If yes, prefer consensus-based stores (etcd/ZK).
- Is latency critical and operations short? Redis SETNX + token may be acceptable.
keyTakeaways: Always include a unique token and atomic release (check-and-delete) to avoid deleting someone else's lock.
Use TTLs to avoid permanent deadlocks, but beware of client pauses and renew carefully or prefer session-backed locks.
For strong correctness under partitions, prefer consensus-backed ephemeral locks (etcd/Zookeeper) and fencing tokens.
